🔖 Binance has confirmed that it is working closely with the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) and cryptocurrency industry partners to recover funds stolen during its October security breach, following the government’s latest action to forfeit more than $1.1 billion in USDC. 📊 “We are coordinating closely with the U.S. Department of Justice, as well as with industry partners who have assisted in freezing assets impacted by the incident,” Binance wrote. “We expect to continue cooperating throughout the asset forfeiture process, with the goal of supporting the return of affected funds as efficiently as possible.” The statement followed an announcement from the FBI’s Cyber Branch that U.S. authorities and private sector companies had collectively assisted in freezing, seizing or returning more than $2.9 billion in cryptocurrency since the October 29 theft.

⚠️ Circle Internet Financial, the issuer of USDC, had voluntarily restricted access to the funds before federal prosecutors obtained a court order. On November 6, Circle informed authorities that it would maintain the restrictions until the forfeiture proceedings concluded or the court instructed it otherwise, provided prosecutors obtained a temporary restraining order. Araghchi also reiterated Iran’s firm positions and perspectives regarding the requirements and frameworks necessary for establishing regional peace.

Crypto Idea

Let’s assume for a moment that the entire story about Jensen Huang’s departure and sudden return was a perfectly executed maneuver that distracted everyone from a much bigger problem inside Nvidia.

Watch closely.

On November 11, Huang steps down as CEO and leaves the board. Nvidia shares crash, dragging the entire AI sector down with them. For a week, the whole world discusses his personal life, an alleged Chinese spy, investigations, and whether he will return.

11 days later, Huang is reinstated. Nvidia surges 31.5% in a single session, recovering nearly $1 trillion in market cap. The Nasdaq 100 gains around 6.6%. Once again, all eyes are on one man.

But what is happening in parallel?

The Financial Times publishes a piece about the circular AI economy. Essentially, it’s about a closed financial loop that has formed around Nvidia and the entire AI industry.

The mechanics are pretty simple.

Nvidia doesn’t just sell chips to its customers. It invests in these companies, helps them secure financing, backs infrastructure projects, and in some cases, even commits to buying computing capacity from them.

These companies get the money, build data centers, and buy Nvidia GPUs. Nvidia generates revenue. That revenue supports Nvidia’s market cap and valuations across the entire AI ecosystem. High valuations make it possible to raise even more money. That money goes toward building new data centers and buying even more Nvidia GPUs.

The loop closes.

According to the Financial Times, the volume of this financing has grown roughly 17-fold over the past three years, approaching $700 billion. Nvidia itself has disclosed more than $500 billion in future financial commitments in its filings. Meanwhile, the SEC is separately examining the company’s accounting amid questions about these types of financing arrangements.

Now, let’s look at Nvidia’s latest earnings report.

Revenue more than doubled, reaching $116 billion for the quarter.

The only question is how much of that growth is driven by independent demand, because actual end-user demand is genuinely massive, and how much is sustained by a system in which the seller of the hardware is also helping its buyers find the money to purchase that same hardware.

As long as the loop keeps spinning upward, the numbers look spectacular.

But if financing starts to dry up, the whole thing could work in reverse. Less money, fewer data centers, fewer GPU orders, lower revenue, lower valuations, and even less financing available.

Now think about that.
